title: Git
description: Save snapshots of your work, read the history, branch safely and merge, conflicts included.

body.text: Git records snapshots of your project over time. Each snapshot is a commit, so you can see what changed, when and why, and go back if something breaks.
Three places a change can be
The working directory holds your files as you edit them. The staging area holds the changes you picked for the next commit. The repository holds the commits.

body.code:
git init      # start tracking this folder
git status    # see what changed

body.text: Run git status often. It always tells you what Git sees and usually suggests the next command.
Committing is a two-step move: first stage the changes, then save them with a message.

body.code:
git add README.md
git commit -m "Add README"

body.text: git add . stages every change in the current folder. git log --oneline lists commits, one per line.
Write messages that say why, in a short line: "Fix login timeout" is more useful than "changes".

questions.prompt: Which command puts a changed file into the staging area?
questions.explanation: git add stages changes. git commit then saves everything that is staged as one snapshot.

questions.prompt: git init needs an internet connection.
questions.explanation: git init only creates a hidden .git folder on your machine. Git works fully offline until you push or pull.

questions.prompt: Type the command that commits staged changes with the message "Add login".
questions.explanation: -m lets you write the commit message on the same line.

options: A saved snapshot of the project with a message
A copy of the project on GitHub
A list of files Git ignores
correctAnswers: A saved snapshot of the project with a message
questions.explanation: Each commit records the staged files at that moment, who made it and why (the message).

labs.title: Your first commit
labs.scenario: This project folder has a README but no version control yet. Turn it into a Git repository and save the first snapshot.
hints: First tell Git to start tracking this folder.
After git init, look at git status, stage the README with git add, then commit with a message.
Type: git init, git status, git add README.md, git commit -m "Add README"

body.text: Git does not save every change by itself. You choose what goes into the next commit by staging it. Think of the staging area as a box you pack before sealing it with a commit.

body.code:
git status              # what changed?
git add login.html      # stage one file
git add .               # stage everything here
git commit -m "Add login page"

body.text: Stage files separately to keep commits small: one idea per commit. Small commits are easier to review and to undo.
Reading history

body.code:
git log --oneline
3f2a91b Add login page
9c1d0e4 Add README
body.caption: Newest first

body.text: git commit -am "message" stages and commits files Git already tracks in one step. Brand new files still need git add.

options: Stages every change in this folder
correctAnswers: Stages every change in this folder
questions.explanation: The dot means the current folder. Nothing is saved until you commit.

questions.prompt: git commit -am also includes brand new files that were never added.
questions.explanation: -a only stages files Git already tracks. New files need git add first.

questions.prompt: Type the command that shows the history with one line per commit.
questions.explanation: --oneline shows the short id and message of each commit.

labs.title: One idea per commit
labs.scenario: Your app has one commit. Add a login page and explain how to run the app in the README, but save them as two separate commits. Then check the history.
hints: Do one change, stage it with git add, commit it, then do the next change.
touch login.html creates the page. echo "Run: npm start" >> README.md adds a line to the README.
Type: touch login.html, git add login.html, git commit -m "Add login page", echo "Run: npm start" >> README.md, git commit -am "Explain how to run", git log --oneline

body.text: A branch is a separate line of work. You can try a feature on a branch without touching main, then merge it when it is ready.

body.code:
git branch            # list branches
git switch -c login   # create and move to a new branch
git switch main       # go back to main

body.text: Older tutorials use git checkout -b login. It does the same as git switch -c login.
Bringing work back

body.code:
git switch main
git merge login

body.text: Commit or stash your changes before switching branches, so nothing gets mixed up.

questions.prompt: Type one command that creates a branch called dev and switches to it.
questions.explanation: Both git switch -c dev and the older git checkout -b dev create the branch and move you onto it.

questions.prompt: You are on main. Which command brings the commits from the login branch into main?
questions.explanation: git merge joins another branch's history into the branch you are on.

questions.prompt: Switching to another branch changes the files you see in the folder.
questions.explanation: git switch makes the folder match the last commit of that branch.

labs.title: Build a feature on a branch
labs.scenario: The app already has one commit on main. Start a login feature on its own branch and commit your work there.
hints: You need a new branch named login, and you need to be on it.
git switch -c creates and switches in one step. Then create a file, stage it and commit.
Type: git switch -c login, touch login.txt, git add login.txt, git commit -m "Start login"

body.text: When work on a branch is ready, merge it. First switch to the branch that should receive the work, then merge the other one into it.

body.code:
git switch main
git merge login

body.text: If main has not moved since the branch started, Git simply moves main forward to the branch's last commit. This is called a fast-forward.
If both branches have new commits, Git makes a merge commit that joins the two histories.
git branch lists your branches; the one with * is where you are.
If both branches changed the same line, Git cannot guess which version is right. It stops and marks the file:

body.caption: Top: your branch. Bottom: the branch being merged

body.text: git status lists the files with conflicts. Fix each one by writing the final version, without the marker lines. Then stage it and commit to finish the merge.

body.code:
echo "

Hello and good day

" > index.html git add index.html git commit -m "Merge new-title"

body.text: Changed your mind? git merge --abort puts everything back the way it was before the merge.

questions.prompt: You want login's work in main. Which branch do you switch to before git merge login?
questions.explanation: You merge INTO the branch you are on. Switch to main, then git merge login.

options: Git moves the branch ahead because nothing else changed
A merge that skips the conflicts
A merge that deletes the other branch
correctAnswers: Git moves the branch ahead because nothing else changed
questions.explanation: No new commits on main means nothing to join, so main just points at the newer commit.

questions.prompt: What does <<<<<<< HEAD mark in a file?
options: The start of your branch's version in a conflict
A comment Git adds to every file
correctAnswers: The start of your branch's version in a conflict
questions.explanation: Between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= is your version; below it, the other branch's version.

questions.prompt: After fixing a conflict you git add the file and commit.
questions.explanation: Staging the fixed file tells Git the conflict is solved; the commit finishes the merge.

questions.prompt: Type the command that cancels a merge that has conflicts.
questions.explanation: --abort returns the files and the branch to how they were before the merge.

labs.title: Ship a feature
labs.scenario: A teammate finished the about page on the about branch. Look at the branches, bring the work into main and check the history.
hints: git branch shows every branch. You are already on main, the branch that should receive the work.
git merge followed by the branch name brings its commits into main.
Type: git branch, then git merge about, then git log --oneline

labs.title: Fix a merge conflict
labs.scenario: You and a teammate both changed the page title. Merge the new-title branch into main, fix the conflict by keeping a title that mixes both, and finish the merge.
hints: Run git merge new-title. It stops with a conflict; git status and cat index.html show you where.
Overwrite index.html with your final title using echo and >, so no <<<<<<< lines are left. Then git add and git commit.

Type: git merge new-title, git status, echo "

Hello and good day

" > index.html, git add index.html, git commit -m "Merge new-title"
